strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored question at the intersection of NLP, HCI, and qualitative research, comparing three substantially different interactive-system paradigms. The manuscript is clear and well organized :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ujg7tx7j/call-578b46f888f34976a17f776c446869ac/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The study represents considerable empirical effort: 33 researchers, 30 reported experimental runs, two contrasting corpora, three systems, and a post-hoc audit of 2,400 document-theme pairs. Reporting Krippendorff's alpha of 0.632 and 0.696 provides useful evidence about the reliability of that audit.

The evaluation considers complementary aspects of the outputs—cross-codebook consistency, within-codebook cohesion/distinctiveness, and manually judged assignment correctness—rather than relying on a single automatic score. The descriptive findings are appropriately heterogeneous and do not simply declare one system universally best.

Reproducibility is aided by a public code/results repository and unusually extensive appendices containing prompts, system operations, dataset statistics, complete codebooks, theme counts, and similarity heatmaps.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. The asynchronous condition is one coder with no reported consolidation, while the synchronous condition is a three-person team; modality is therefore confounded with team size, total person-effort, and consensus formation. Participant reuse was not counterbalanced—repeat participants always completed asynchronous work first—and assignment, expertise balance, and session duration are not reported. With only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per system-dataset cell, the claim that modality significantly affects quality is unsupported.

The inferential statistics in Tables 1 and 2 are not credible as presented. The unit of analysis and test sample sizes are unspecified; treating themes or document pairs as independent observations would be pseudoreplication because they are nested within only 2–3 codebooks. Approximately 42 uncorrected comparisons are made, without confidence intervals or a hierarchical analysis, and even tiny differences are called significant. The paper's main significance claims therefore cannot be distinguished from coder/session variation.

The proposed quality measures lack sufficient construct validation. Maximum best-match alignment is not specified as symmetric or one-to-one, can map several themes to the same broad theme, and is inflated by differing codebook sizes (7–25 themes). Centroid similarities are nearly saturated at 0.89–0.98 without a null baseline. Cohesion and separation in embedding space are not necessarily measures of good inductive qualitative analysis, while selecting the closest 25% of documents mechanically improves cohesion.

The correctness evaluation omits confidence intervals and statistical tests despite claiming significant superiority in Figure 4. Sampling allocation across sessions and themes, evaluator identity/blinding, adjudication details, and treatment of unmapped outputs are unclear. This is especially consequential because the LLM leaves up to 16.1% of documents unlabeled; evaluating only successful assignments would overstate its quality.

The qualitative component is anecdotal rather than a reproducible user study: no number of analyzed interviews, transcription procedure, coding method, analyst agreement, or prevalence of themes is given. Synchronous participants were interviewed in groups while asynchronous participants were interviewed individually, introducing another condition-dependent confound.

Claims about dataset characteristics and intervention richness are post-hoc extrapolations from only two datasets and one implementation of each system class. The corpora simultaneously differ in domain, size, length, formulaicity, and available auxiliary labels, so effects cannot be attributed to any identified property. Both are English-language US political corpora, further limiting generalization.

Important reproducibility inconsistencies remain despite the released artifacts: the exact SBERT checkpoint, random seeds, Llama decoding parameters, participant/session mapping, and several clustering settings are absent. Prompt selection has no held-out validation and yields low Gwet's AC1 values of 0.25–0.62. Moreover, all five Climate relational and LLM codebooks in Tables 15–16 are verbatim identical apart from ordering, without explanation, and Table 10's “similarity > 0.3” row contradicts the accompanying prose.

These concerns affect the validity of the principal findings, not merely presentation or prospective impact, so the paper does not yet meet the soundness threshold for Findings. A next-cycle resubmission could be viable if framed as an exploratory case study with session-level uncertainty, substantially tempered claims, clarified artifacts, and preferably a balanced replication.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely, clearly NLP-relevant question about collaborative qualitative analysis with human-in-the-loop systems.
The empirical scope is ambitious: three distinct tool paradigms, two contrasting corpora, 33 participants, 2,400 human-evaluated assignments, and complementary quantitative and interview evidence.

Prompts, system operations, final codebooks, several hyperparameters, and a public code/data repository provide useful transparency. The presentation is generally clear and the conclusions acknowledge that no configuration is uniformly best.
Reporting both full-theme and high-confidence-subset results is potentially informative, and the paper surfaces practical concerns about user control and large-scale LLM annotation.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration. Each synchronous output is produced by a three-person team, whereas each asynchronous output is produced by one person without the stated consolidation stage. Modality is therefore inseparable from team size, total labor, and consensus formation; the experiment is more accurately a comparison of synchronous teams with solo coders.

There are only two synchronous sessions and three asynchronous sessions per system-dataset cell. Participants are reused, always perform asynchronous work first, and are not reported as randomized, counterbalanced, or balanced by expertise. Session/codebook is the relevant experimental unit, so the study cannot support reliable population-level modality effects without substantially more independent groups.

The statistical analysis is not soundly specified. The unit supplied to each unpaired t-test is unstated; treating themes or document pairs as independent constitutes pseudoreplication, while using the actual 2-versus-3 session sample is inadequate. The paper also performs dozens of comparisons without multiplicity control and omits exact p-values, test statistics, confidence intervals, and effect sizes. Table 2 even marks rounded-equal values as significantly different. Consequently, the significance-based central claims are unsupported.

The proposed consistency metric uses independent maximum matches rather than a one-to-one alignment, allowing several themes to match the same counterpart and largely ignoring unmatched themes despite codebook sizes ranging from 7 to 25. Its directionality and aggregation across codebook pairs are unclear. SBERT cohesion and distinctiveness are also not validated as measures of qualitative-code quality and can reward lexical clustering rather than interpretive validity; the top-25% comparison additionally uses different ranking mechanisms across systems.

The correctness evaluation is insufficiently defined. Figure 4 reports F1, but the paper never explains the positive and negative instances, how recall is obtained from sampled assigned pairs, or how scores are aggregated across themes and sessions. Allocation of only 200 pairs per setting, treatment of uncovered or hallucinated labels, evaluator blinding, and uncertainty are unspecified. Claims of significant differences have no reported tests or error bars, while agreement is only moderate (Krippendorff's alpha 0.632 and 0.696).

Claims about effects of dataset characteristics are observational and post hoc. The two corpora simultaneously differ in domain, size, length, formulaicity, labels, and many other properties, so no individual characteristic—and certainly no independent dataset effect—can be identified. Several explanations are speculative, and Table 10's stated greater-than-0.3 percentages contradict the accompanying prose.

The LLM analysis selects prompts on the same human-labeled data used to score them, reports low Gwet AC1 values of 0.25–0.62, and produces invalid labels for up to 16.1% of documents without explaining their downstream treatment. Exact SBERT checkpoints, preprocessing, random seeds, LLM decoding parameters, and several sampling details are absent. The verbatim-identical Climate codebooks in Tables 15 and 16 also require clarification about reuse and independence of the relational and LLM experiments.

The interview component is not rigorous enough to substantiate its findings: the number of interviews, participant selection, transcription and coding procedure, analyst agreement, theme frequencies, and negative cases are unreported. Moreover, synchronous participants are interviewed in groups while asynchronous participants are interviewed individually, confounding condition with elicitation method.

Repairing the decisive problems requires a balanced asynchronous-team condition with consolidation, controlled effort and participant assignment, more independent sessions, and a hierarchical or session-level analysis. This is substantial new experimental work rather than a next-cycle presentation revision.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, under-evaluated question at the intersection of NLP, HCI, and qualitative research, with ambitious coverage of three interactive-system paradigms and two distinct corpora. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-v1n9l3wo/call-400959eb6fe34fea95e1995ab5225aca/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed evaluation triangulates document overlap, semantic cohesion/distinctiveness, manual assessment of 2,400 assignments, and participant interviews. This is appreciably richer than relying on topic coherence alone.

The paper is generally clear and unusually transparent about prompts, compute, final codebooks, participant composition, and several corpus characteristics; it also states that code and experimental data are public.

The empirical observations are appropriately nuanced in one respect: no system or collaboration setting dominates across datasets, highlighting potentially useful interactions among workflow, model affordances, and corpus properties.
weaknesses: The experiment does not isolate collaboration modality. Each asynchronous output is produced by one individual and is never consolidated, whereas each synchronous output is produced by three people deliberating together. Thus modality is confounded with group size, labor, and aggregation; the purported asynchronous condition is not asynchronous collaboration as defined in the introduction. Allocation, time budgets, and condition-level expertise are unreported, while repeat participants always perform asynchronous work first, introducing additional selection, order, and carryover confounds.

The inferential analysis cannot support the central claims. There are only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous individuals per system-dataset cell, with further dependence from repeated participants. The paper does not identify the unit used in its unpaired t-tests. Treating themes or the many document pairs as observations is pseudoreplication; treating codebooks as observations leaves only n=2 versus n=3. Exact p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, multiplicity correction, and a hierarchical analysis are absent. Consequently, stars on very small differences and claims of significant modality effects are not credible.

The consistency metric has serious construct-validity problems: independent maximum matching is potentially asymmetric and many-to-one, rewards redundant or broad themes, and is mechanically affected by the number of candidate themes, which ranges from 7 to 25. Near-saturated centroid similarities do little to discriminate codebooks. Cohesion metrics are not normalized against corpus baselines, theme size, or overlap, and selecting the top quartile with the same embedding geometry subsequently used for evaluation is circular. These measures therefore need validation before being presented as a standardized framework.

The correctness and interview components are under-specified. The paper does not report a sufficiently precise correctness rubric, evaluator identities and blinding, sampling allocation across unequal codebooks, per-condition agreement, uncertainty, or statistical comparisons; the cumulative-quartile plot further obscures independent strata. For the interviews, it omits participant counts by condition, recording/transcription procedures, analysis method, number of qualitative coders, agreement or reflexivity practices, prevalence of reported themes, and negative cases. A few selected quotations cannot substantiate the broad design recommendations.

Important reproducibility and dependency questions remain despite the stated artifact release. Exact SBERT checkpoints, preprocessing, clustering seeds, LLM decoding settings, and handling of missing or overlapping assignments are not specified. Prompt selection is performed on the same human-labeled examples rather than held-out data, agreement is only 0.25–0.62, and 0.7–16.1% of LLM outputs use labels outside the codebook; how these failures enter each metric is unclear. Moreover, Tables 15 and 16 contain exactly the same five climate codebooks for the relational and LLM systems despite the text describing separate experiments, leaving reuse and experimental independence unexplained. Table 10 also contradicts its surrounding text about similarity below versus above 0.3.

These are decisive soundness concerns, not merely limitations in novelty or scale. The study offers interesting exploratory observations, but its stated causal and general claims are unsupported across only two US political corpora and a convenience sample. Establishing the claimed collaboration effect requires genuine matched asynchronous teams, substantially more independent group replications, controlled effort and assignment, and group-aware analysis—or a major reframing as a descriptive case study with appropriately limited claims. This likely exceeds a next-cycle revision.

strengths: Addresses an important, underexplored ACL/HCI question: how collaborative workflows interact with NLP-assisted qualitative coding. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-o5eyau7s/call-e359d1d4e8ca4c34a6ca70f3b9114d72/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical scope is ambitious: 33 researchers, three substantially different interactive systems, two corpora, 30 coding sessions, and 2,400 post-hoc assignment judgments.
Evaluating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness provides a useful multidimensional perspective beyond conventional topic-coherence evaluation.
The paper is generally clear and supplies extensive codebooks, prompts, per-session LLM agreement and missing-label statistics, plus a public code/data link.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not identify an effect of collaboration modality: every asynchronous condition has one coder, whereas every synchronous condition has three. Thus modality is confounded with group size, total human effort, and deliberation; moreover, the asynchronous condition includes no team or consolidation stage despite being described as asynchronous collaboration.

There are only two independent synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system-dataset cell. Some participants recur, always doing asynchronous work first, and randomization or balancing is not reported. The unpaired t-tests apparently use nested theme- or document-level measurements as independent observations, rather than the session/group as the experimental unit. This pseudoreplication, combined with many uncorrected tests, no exact p-values or confidence intervals, and references to “near significance,” makes the inferential claims unreliable.

The maximum-overlap consistency measure permits many-to-one matches and is not clearly symmetrized. It is consequently inflated by codebook size, which varies markedly across sessions (7–25 themes), and the treatment of unassigned documents is unclear.

Embedding compactness is not established as a valid proxy for qualitative theme quality. SBERT also participates in constructing the relational system's clusters and assignments, then evaluates those outputs, creating methodological dependence. Several statistically highlighted cohesion differences are only 0.01, yet the discussion describes them as substantial.

The correctness analysis is under-specified: Figure 4 reports F1 without defining predictions, reference labels, or averaging; sampling allocation across sessions and themes is unclear; evaluator blinding is unreported; and there are no uncertainty intervals or documented significance tests. Differential LLM failure rates of 0.7%–16.1% unlabeled documents could materially bias these results, but their handling is not explained.

Claims about the effects of dataset characteristics are not supported by a two-dataset comparison in which topic, platform, corpus size, document length, formulaicity, and semantics all change together. Recommendations tying collaboration mode to homogeneity or complexity are therefore post-hoc hypotheses, not independently demonstrated findings.

The interview component lacks essential qualitative-method details, including interview count and duration, transcription, analysis/coding procedure, researcher reflexivity, and prevalence of reported views. Conducting synchronous interviews in groups but asynchronous interviews individually further confounds the responses.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the repository: the exact SBERT checkpoint, random seeds, several clustering/GMM choices, LLM decoding settings, participant allocation, and session time budgets are absent. Table 10 also labels values as proportions above 0.3 while the prose interprets them as below 0.3. Fixing the central evidential problem likely requires either new controlled replication or a major reframing as a descriptive exploratory case study.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored question at the intersection of NLP, HCI, and qualitative research: how collaborative workflows interact with NLP-assisted theme discovery. Comparing topic-model, relational, and LLM-based systems on two substantially different corpora is relevant and potentially useful.

The study represents considerable empirical effort: 33 researchers, 30 coding sessions, multiple complementary quality dimensions, 2,400 post-hoc document-theme judgments, and reported inter-annotator reliability. Examining consistency, cohesion, distinctiveness, and correctness separately usefully reveals that no configuration dominates on every criterion.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. Its appendices report prompts, resulting codebooks, compute requirements, dataset diagnostics, and participant-facing operations, while a public code/data link improves transparency. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-tep7brxg/call-a0e002ee78134a65a9120a4b028868c0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Each asynchronous outcome comes from one coder, whereas each synchronous outcome comes from three coders working jointly; person-hours and stopping times are not reported or matched. Moreover, the asynchronous condition contains no team consolidation despite this being part of the paper's own definition of asynchronous collaboration. Participant assignment is not described as randomized, some participants repeat experiments, and asynchronous participation always occurs first. Differences can therefore arise from team size, effort, composition, or order effects rather than synchronicity.

There is insufficient independent replication for the inferential claims: each system-dataset cell has only three asynchronous individuals and two synchronous groups, yielding only one synchronous codebook-pair for consistency. The unit used in the unpaired t-tests is not specified; the reported standard deviations and numerous significant results, including for differences of 0.01, appear to treat nested themes or document pairs as independent observations. Exact p-values, confidence intervals, group-level effect sizes, power analysis, and multiple-comparison correction are absent. Consequently, claims of statistically significant modality effects are not supported.

The proposed metrics have important unaddressed biases. Maximum best-match alignment is neither stated to be symmetric nor one-to-one, does not penalize unmatched themes, and favors codebooks offering more candidate themes; observed codebook sizes range from 7 to 25. SBERT is used both to construct parts of the relational pipeline and to evaluate semantic cohesion, making that evaluation partly circular. Intra/inter-theme similarity is also not normalized against corpus-level baselines or controlled for theme size, and the framework is not validated against independent expert judgments of codebook quality.

The dataset and system conclusions exceed the design. The two corpora differ simultaneously in domain, platform, size, length, formulaicity, and available auxiliary labels, so their effects cannot be attributed to particular dataset characteristics or described as independent. Likewise, one implementation per method family and one small LLM cannot establish general properties of topic-model, relational, or LLM systems. Correctness itself shows no consistent collaboration effect, and the proposed relationship between intervention richness and synchronous benefit is observationally confounded with system identity.

The correctness analysis lacks uncertainty estimates and does not explain evaluator identity, blinding, adjudication guidelines, or allocation of the 200 examples across codebooks. LLM human-model agreement is often low (Gwet's AC1 of 0.25–0.62), and 0.7%–16.1% of documents receive invalid labels. It is unclear how this differential missing coverage enters consistency, cohesion, or correctness; sampling only valid document-theme pairs would overstate performance.

The interview component is not reported as a rigorous qualitative study: the number interviewed, analysis/coding method, analyst agreement, saturation, prevalence of themes, and modality-specific evidence are missing. Synchronous participants were interviewed in groups while asynchronous participants were interviewed individually, adding another confound. A few illustrative quotations cannot support the broad design recommendations.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including the exact SBERT checkpoint, seeds and clustering settings, LLM decoding parameters, participant-to-condition allocation and reuse, session duration or effort budget, and operational stopping criteria. There is also an apparent error in Table 10, whose “similarity > 0.3” row contradicts the accompanying text. These are secondary to the identification and statistical problems: as written, the evidence falls below Findings; a viable revision needs major claim narrowing and reanalysis, while the stated causal/general claims require a better-controlled, adequately replicated study.

strengths: Addresses an important, underexplored CL/HCI question: how collaborative workflows interact with NLP-assisted qualitative coding.

The study represents substantial empirical effort, covering 33 researchers, three distinct system families, two contrasting corpora, and 30 coding sessions. This breadth provides useful exploratory observations.
The multidimensional evaluation—consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, manual assignment assessment, and interviews—is preferable to relying on a single automatic metric.

The paper is generally clear and auditable. The appendices provide prompts, codebooks, system operations, corpus diagnostics, compute information, and LLM coverage statistics, while code and experimental data are reportedly public.
weaknesses: The decisive validity problem is that the experiment does not isolate synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration. Synchronous outputs are produced jointly by three-person teams, whereas asynchronous outputs are produced by single coders without the stated consolidation stage. Collaboration modality is therefore confounded with team size, discussion, total human effort, and aggregation. Participant reuse, with asynchronous participation always preceding synchronous participation, adds an order/experience confound.

There are only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per system-dataset cell. The reported unpaired t-tests appear to treat themes or document-pair similarities as independent observations, although the intervention occurs at the coding-session level. Themes are nested within codebooks, asynchronous pairwise comparisons share codebooks, and document pairs are highly dependent. This pseudoreplication, combined with extensive testing, no multiplicity correction, and no session-level confidence intervals, makes the statistical-significance claims unreliable.

The consistency metric uses unrestricted maximum matching, apparently without guaranteed symmetry, one-to-one alignment, or penalties for unmatched themes. It is consequently sensitive to codebook size, which ranges from 7 to 25 themes. The SBERT measures lack chance or noninteractive baselines, and selecting the top quartile by centroid distance before measuring embedding cohesion is partly circular.

The correctness evaluation is insufficiently specified. The paper does not explain how judgments of sampled positive document-theme pairs produce the F1 scores in Figure 4, how samples are allocated across codebooks and themes, whether evaluators are independent and blinded, or how uncertainty is calculated. It also does not explain whether invalid/unlabeled LLM outputs—up to 16.1% for one codebook—are counted as failures; excluding them would overstate performance.

Claims about effects of dataset characteristics are not identified by the design. The two corpora simultaneously differ in domain, size, length, formulaicity, semantics, and available auxiliary labels, so observations from two data points cannot establish which property caused a system or collaboration effect. The resulting workflow recommendations should be presented as hypotheses rather than supported conclusions.

Important reproducibility details remain absent or ambiguous, including participant allocation and expertise by condition, session duration and action counts, the exact SBERT checkpoint and preprocessing, clustering seeds, relational-model thresholds, LLM decoding parameters, and the precise statistical units. Moreover, Tables 15 and 16 contain identical Climate codebooks for the relational and LLM conditions despite the description of separate experiments; any reuse must be explained because it affects independence.

The interview component lacks the methodological detail needed to support its claims: the number interviewed, recording/transcription procedure, qualitative analysis method, coders, reliability or reflexivity process, and saturation are not reported. Group interviews for synchronous participants versus individual interviews for asynchronous participants also introduce a response-setting confound.

There are smaller interpretation and reporting issues, including labeling Table 10 percentages as similarity greater than 0.3 when the prose indicates they are below 0.3, highlighting “near significance,” and treating moderate Krippendorff alpha values as sufficient without propagating annotation uncertainty. Overall, the work is promising as an exploratory case study, but corrected inference, substantially narrower claims, and preferably additional balanced session-level replication are needed before it meets the Findings soundness threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important, under-studied NLP/HCI question about collaboration in human-in-the-loop qualitative coding. Studying three system families, two real corpora, and 33 relevant researchers is ambitious.

The evaluation considers cross-codebook consistency, within-codebook cohesion/distinctiveness, human-audited assignment correctness, and participant interviews rather than relying on one intrinsic metric.

The paper is clearly organized and unusually transparent about prompts, codebooks, theme counts, corpus diagnostics, and system configurations. It also reports mixed results and provides public code and experimental data.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Synchronous outputs come from teams of three, whereas asynchronous outputs come from single coders without the consolidation step used in the paper's own definition of asynchronous collaboration. Team size, total labor, interaction, and aggregation therefore change simultaneously. Repeated participation and the fixed asynchronous-first order add further confounding.

Statistical inference is not credible at the available level of replication: each system-dataset condition has only two synchronous and three asynchronous independent codebooks. The paper does not state what observations enter its t-tests; significance for differences as small as 0.44 versus 0.43 strongly suggests that dependent theme- or document-level values are treated as independent. There is no multiplicity correction, exact p-values, confidence intervals, or suitable hierarchical analysis.

Claims about dataset characteristics are drawn from only two corpora that differ simultaneously in domain, size, length, formulaicity, and semantic structure. These data cannot establish that any particular characteristic independently causes the observed behavior, yet the conclusions make corpus-level workflow recommendations.

The proposed metrics lack adequate construct validation. Maximum many-to-one theme matching can reward broad or duplicate themes and is sensitive to codebook size, which ranges from 7 to 25 themes. SBERT geometry is also used both to construct assignments in the relational system and to evaluate their quality, introducing circularity and potentially favoring that system.

The correctness audit does not clearly define how binary document-theme judgments yield F1, report class balance or uncertainty, or assess missing themes and codebook completeness. Agreement is only moderate (Krippendorff's alpha 0.632/0.696). The interview findings likewise lack a documented qualitative-analysis procedure, coding reliability, or systematic attribution of evidence.

Although releasing code and outputs helps, reproducibility of the human study is limited by missing participant-to-condition assignments, session/time controls, interaction histories, randomization details, and some model-decoding/statistical specifications.

The causal claims and significance conclusions cannot be repaired through presentation changes alone; they require a redesigned, properly replicated study with comparable group composition and a genuine asynchronous-consolidation condition. This precludes Findings-level soundness and likely requires more than one review cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and understudied NLP/HCI question: how collaborative workflow interacts with NLP-assisted qualitative coding.

The empirical scope is unusually broad for an interactive-system study, covering three distinct system families, two substantially different corpora, 33 researchers, 30 sessions, and released code and experimental outputs.

Evaluating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and human-judged correctness is more informative than relying on a single topic-coherence metric. The 2,400 doubly annotated correctness judgments and reported inter-annotator agreement are valuable.
The systems, protocols, prompts, codebooks, participant feedback, and computational requirements are presented clearly, with useful appendices and generally effective figures.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. The asynchronous condition consists of single coders producing separate codebooks, without the stated consolidation stage, whereas the synchronous condition uses teams of three. Modality is therefore confounded with team size, deliberation, and total labor. Some participants also completed multiple sessions, always asynchronous first, introducing an uncontrolled order/learning confound. The evidence supports an exploratory comparison of individuals and synchronous teams, not the claimed effect of synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration.

There are only two independent synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system-dataset cell. The manuscript does not state the observational unit used in its t-tests; the reported standard deviations and significance markings appear to treat nested theme- or document-level scores as independent. Such pseudoreplication cannot support population-level modality claims. Exact p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, power analysis, and multiple-comparison correction are absent despite dozens of tests, and some statistically marked differences are only 0.01.

The proposed metrics have unresolved validity problems. Maximum many-to-one theme matching is insufficiently specified, is biased by the substantially different codebook sizes, and can match several themes to the same counterpart. SBERT geometry is used both in constructing some system outputs and in evaluating their semantic quality; selecting the top quartile by centroid distance and then measuring embedding cohesion is particularly circular. No random-partition, human-only, or expert-quality baseline establishes that these embedding quantities measure qualitative-analysis quality, where interpretive themes need not form compact semantic clusters.

The correctness evaluation is not reproducible from the description. The paper samples system-assigned document-theme pairs but reports F1 without explaining how false negatives or recall are obtained. It also omits annotation guidelines, evaluator identities and blinding, per-codebook sample allocation, uncertainty estimates, significance procedures, and treatment of unmapped or invalid outputs. LLM runs have Gwet agreement as low as 0.25 and up to 16.1% invalid labels, making coverage handling especially consequential.

Claims about dataset characteristics are post-hoc and overgeneralized. The study has only two corpora that simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, document length, formulaicity, semantic diversity, and available auxiliary labels, so none of these factors can be isolated. Likewise, one implementation per system family cannot establish conclusions about topic models, relational methods, or LLMs generally.

The interview component reports neither the number of interviews nor a qualitative coding procedure, analyst agreement, prevalence of findings, or negative cases; a few quotations cannot substantiate the broad design recommendations. Several reporting gaps further limit reproducibility, including the exact SBERT checkpoint, random seeds, decoding parameters, participant allocation, session duration, metric aggregation, and held-out prompt selection. Table 10 also labels values as percentages above 0.3 while the text interprets them as percentages below 0.3. Addressing the decisive design and independent-replication problems would require more than editorial clarification, so the current paper is not yet sound enough for Findings.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a timely, CL-relevant question at the intersection of human-in-the-loop NLP and qualitative analysis. Its breadth—three substantially different systems, two real-world corpora, 30 sessions, and 33 participants—gives the study considerable potential value. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8e1fkm09/call-fe651441f49a4244a7457ee1fd9eb2d0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed evaluation is commendably multidimensional: document-overlap and semantic consistency, cohesion/distinctiveness, manual assessment of 2,400 assignments, and participant interviews provide complementary perspectives rather than relying on one automatic score.

The paper is generally clear and unusually transparent about prompts, final codebooks, participant demographics, model compute, and human agreement. Public code and experimental data further improve its reproducibility prospects.
The heterogeneous descriptive results are useful: they caution against assuming one tool or workflow is universally best and motivate studying interactions among interfaces, users, and corpora.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration. Each “asynchronous” session has one coder and no consolidation, whereas each synchronous session has three coders. Thus modality is confounded with team size, deliberation, and total human labor; the asynchronous condition is individual coding, not asynchronous collaboration as defined in the introduction. Repeated participation, fixed asynchronous-before-synchronous ordering, absent randomization information, and no controlled time/effort budget add further confounds. Consequently, the claimed effect of collaboration modality is not established.

The inferential statistics appear to use non-independent themes or document pairs as observations. For each dataset-system combination there are only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks—and only one pair of synchronous codebooks for the consistency analysis—yet numerous tiny differences are declared significant using unpaired t-tests. The paper does not state the test unit, sample size, degrees of freedom, exact p-values, confidence intervals, or multiplicity correction, and even highlights “near statistically significant” results. This likely constitutes pseudoreplication and invalidates the principal significance claims.

The proposed metrics are insufficiently validated as measures of qualitative-analysis quality. Maximum many-to-one theme matching is sensitive to codebook size and granularity and is not clearly symmetric; codebook sizes vary substantially. SBERT cohesion can reward lexical homogeneity rather than interpretive quality, while selecting the top quartile by centroid distance partly guarantees increased cohesion. Null baselines, sensitivity analyses, balanced matching, and validation against expert judgments are missing.

The “correctness” analysis is under-specified. Figure 4 reports F1 without defining positives, negatives, precision, or recall; sampling only assigned document-theme pairs would estimate precision, not F1. No uncertainty intervals or statistical tests are shown, and annotator instructions, blinding, sample allocation, and treatment of uncovered documents are unclear. This matters because LLM agreement is only 0.25–0.62 and 0.7–16.1% of documents receive invalid/unseen labels, yet coverage is not incorporated into the main comparisons.

Claims that dataset characteristics independently determine workflow performance are not supported by only two corpora, for which domain, platform, size, length, formulaicity, and semantic diversity are all confounded. Section 5.4 is therefore post-hoc hypothesis generation rather than causal evidence. Table 10 also appears mislabeled: its “similarity > 0.3” row conflicts with the accompanying text describing percentages below 0.3.

The interview component lacks the analysis needed for a qualitative user study: the number of interviews, transcription/coding procedure, analyst agreement or reflexivity, and evidence supporting each theme are not reported, while parts of the script are leading and synchronous participants were interviewed in groups. The resulting recommendations rest mainly on a few anecdotes.

Important reproducibility details remain absent, including the exact SBERT checkpoint, seeds, preprocessing, clustering and inference settings, LLM decoding parameters, participant allocation, session duration, and metric aggregation. Moreover, Tables 15 and 16 contain exactly the same five Climate codebooks for the relational and LLM systems despite the study describing separate system-specific experiments; whether codebooks were reused or this is a reporting error must be clarified. The study is promising, but a sound Findings case requires substantial reframing or a matched asynchronous-collaboration condition, session-level statistical analysis with more independent groups, and a corrected, fully specified evaluation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexamined NLP/HCI question: how collaborative workflows interact with human-in-the-loop qualitative coding systems.
The empirical effort is substantial, involving 33 researchers, three distinct system paradigms, two corpora, 30 reported coding experiments, and manual assessment of 2,400 document-theme pairs.

Considering consistency, cohesion, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness is more informative than relying on a single topic-quality metric. The paper also appropriately observes that no system or workflow is uniformly best.
The manuscript is generally clear and provides useful appendices containing prompts, resulting codebooks, operational details, and corpus analyses. Code and experimental data are linked publicly.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Synchronous codebooks are produced by three-person teams, whereas asynchronous codebooks are produced by individual coders, apparently without the consolidation stage used to define asynchronous collaboration. Synchrony is therefore confounded with team size, total labor, and collective expertise. Supporting the causal claim would require same-sized teams, comparable consolidation procedures and effort, and randomized or counterbalanced assignment.

There are only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders for each tool-dataset condition. The paper does not identify the observations supplied to its unpaired t-tests. Testing theme-level or document-pair-level measurements would constitute pseudoreplication because themes and documents are nested within only 2 versus 3 independent sessions. Exact p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, multiplicity correction, and a session-level analysis are absent, yet numerous small differences are called significant.

The proposed metrics have major construct-validity problems. Maximum many-to-one theme matching is asymmetric or insufficiently specified, does not penalize unmatched or redundant themes, and is biased by the sharply varying codebook sizes of 7–25 themes. SBERT centroid similarities of 0.89–0.98 offer little discrimination, and embedding cohesion or coder consistency is not independently validated as codebook quality or qualitative usefulness.

The correctness evaluation is underdefined. The paper reports F1 after sampling assigned document-theme pairs but does not explain the prediction/reference construction needed to calculate F1, sampling allocation across codebooks, adjudication criteria, annotator blinding, uncertainty, or significance tests. It also does not explain how systematically different rates of invalid LLM labels—0.7% to 16.1%—enter the reported metrics.

Claims about dataset characteristics are post-hoc speculation from only two corpora that simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, length, formulaicity, and available auxiliary concepts. These factors cannot be disentangled, so recommendations that heterogeneous corpora benefit from asynchronous coding are not supported. Likewise, one implementation per broad method family—and one 3B LLM with modest human-model agreement—cannot support general conclusions about topic models, relational methods, or LLMs.

Participant allocation, experience balance, session duration, compensation, system and dataset order, and repeated-participant dependencies are not adequately reported or controlled. Requiring repeated participants to perform asynchronous work first introduces rather than eliminates possible learning and carryover effects.

The qualitative interview component lacks the number of interviewees, transcription and coding procedures, analyst agreement or reflexivity, and evidence linking themes to participants. Individual asynchronous interviews and group synchronous interviews also introduce a modality-specific reporting and social-desirability confound.

There are consequential reproducibility and reporting gaps despite the released repository: the exact SBERT checkpoint, preprocessing, random seeds, K-means settings, LLM decoding configuration, prompt selected for each run, and handling of missing outputs are not specified. Moreover, the climate codebooks in Appendix Tables 15 and 16 are identical for the relational and LLM experiments, without explaining whether annotations were reused or whether this is a reporting error. Table 10 also labels values as percentages above 0.3 while the surrounding text interprets them as percentages below 0.3.

Overall, the study supplies potentially valuable exploratory observations, but its central causal claims and significance statements are not validly supported. A credible resubmission would likely require a redesigned, adequately replicated user study rather than a next-cycle textual revision or simple reanalysis.

strengths: Addresses an important, under-studied NLP/HCI question: how collaborative workflows interact with NLP-assisted qualitative coding. Comparing topic-model, relational, and LLM-based systems on two corpora is ambitious and relevant to ACL.

Triangulates several forms of evidence—cross-coder consistency, semantic cohesiveness/distinctiveness, manually assessed assignment correctness, and participant interviews—rather than relying on one automatic metric.

The paper is generally clear and provides useful appendices containing prompts, complete codebooks, dataset analyses, and computational details. Public code and experimental data are also stated to be available.

The mixed findings are potentially informative: the paper does not simply declare one system universally superior and usefully highlights user control, corpus characteristics, and LLM cost and reliability as practical concerns.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. A synchronous condition is a live three-person team, whereas an asynchronous condition is one coder working alone; the described asynchronous consolidation step is never evaluated. Group size, total human effort, participant composition, and interaction are therefore inseparable from synchrony. Participant reuse, assignment, session duration, expertise balance, and counterbalancing are insufficiently reported, and always running asynchronous sessions first permits learning effects. Supporting the causal claim requires a substantially redesigned study with comparable teams and effort.

The inferential statistics appear invalid at the level of the intervention. There are only two synchronous teams and three asynchronous individuals per system-dataset combination; consistency between the two synchronous codebooks yields only one independent comparison. Nevertheless, unpaired t-tests apparently treat themes or document pairs as independent observations, producing significance even for differences of 0.01 or values identical after rounding. This is pseudoreplication, compounded by many uncorrected tests, absent exact p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes.

The proposed quality metrics have major construct-validity problems. Maximum theme matching permits many-to-one alignments and apparently neither penalizes unmatched themes nor clearly defines symmetry. SBERT-based cohesion rewards embedding geometry rather than necessarily valid qualitative themes and partly evaluates systems using the same representation involved in constructing their outputs. Results are also confounded by codebook size, assignment cardinality, and differing coverage; the system-specific top-25% selection procedures further prevent clean comparison. Several statistically marked differences are practically negligible and are overstated as substantially better outcomes.

The correctness evaluation is under-specified: the allocation of 2,400 judgments across 30 experiments is unclear, and the paper does not report a detailed rubric, evaluator independence or blinding, per-condition uncertainty, or inferential tests. Krippendorff's alpha is only moderate. LLM agreement is frequently low (AC1 0.25–0.62), and up to 16.1% of documents receive invalid labels, yet it is unclear how these failures and unmapped relational-system documents enter correctness and other metrics.

Claims about dataset characteristics are not identifiable from two corpora that simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, length, formulaicity, and available auxiliary labels. These observational differences cannot establish that any characteristic independently caused system performance or justify the proposed general prescription for homogeneous versus heterogeneous corpora. Table 10 also conflicts with its accompanying prose about proportions above versus below the similarity threshold.

There is a serious unexplained internal inconsistency: every Climate codebook and theme count in the relational condition is exactly reproduced, merely reordered, in the purportedly separate LLM condition; some COVID codebooks are likewise duplicated or subsets. This is incompatible with the stated design of separate experiments unless codebooks were deliberately reused, which is not disclosed. It raises concerns about independence, carryover, or reporting accuracy.

The interview component cannot substantiate its thematic conclusions: no transcription or qualitative-analysis procedure, coder counts, prevalence, saturation analysis, or reliability process is described, and synchronous participants were interviewed in groups while asynchronous participants were interviewed individually. The evidence presented is largely a few selected quotations.

Overall, the study offers a promising research direction and useful descriptive material, but its causal claims and statistical evidence are not presently sound. Repair requires new, adequately replicated and controlled human-subject experiments rather than a paper-only revision, motivating a 1.5 assessment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored NLP/HCI question: how collaborative workflow interacts with human-in-the-loop qualitative coding systems.
The empirical scope is ambitious, covering three substantially different system paradigms, two contrasting corpora, 33 researchers, and a 2,400-pair manual audit.

The proposed evaluation considers complementary properties—cross-codebook consistency, within-codebook cohesion/distinctiveness, and assignment correctness—rather than relying on topic coherence alone.
The appendices expose prompts, codebooks, system operations, and corpus analyses, and the stated release of code and experimental data is valuable for transparency.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not identify an effect of collaboration modality. The synchronous condition uses three-person teams, whereas each asynchronous condition uses one coder and never performs the consolidation that the paper itself includes in its definition of asynchronous collaboration. Modality is therefore confounded with team size, total human input, and collective decision-making; this is principally a team-versus-individual comparison.

There are only two independent synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders for each system–dataset condition. The unit used in the reported unpaired t-tests is not specified. Testing theme- or document-pair-level observations would be severe pseudoreplication, while testing the actual experimental units would be essentially unpowered. The significance of differences as small as 0.01 in Table 2 strongly suggests the former. Exact sample sizes, p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, and multiple-comparison correction are absent, and highlighting “near significance” is inappropriate.

Participant allocation is insufficiently controlled and internally unclear. Some participants completed multiple experiments, asynchronous participation always preceded synchronous participation, and neither randomization nor matching by expertise is reported. Thus participant composition and learning/order effects can explain observed differences. Moreover, 12 three-person synchronous experiments require 36 synchronous coder slots, which conflicts with 33 participants each reportedly joining at most one synchronous experiment unless some sessions or codebooks were shared; the extensive identity between relational and LLM codebooks is also unexplained.

The metric validity is not established. Maximum-over-theme matching is not a one-to-one alignment, may be asymmetric, and is sensitive to the widely varying number and granularity of themes. SBERT similarity primarily measures embedding/lexical compactness, not qualitative interpretive quality. Selecting the top 25% of documents by centroid proximity makes increased cohesion partly tautological and is implemented differently for the topic model.

The correctness analysis is not reproducible or adequately justified: Figure 4 reports an undefined F1 score, although only assigned document–theme pairs appear to be sampled; negative examples, aggregation, annotator blinding, and uncertainty are unspecified. LLM invalid/unlabeled outputs reach 16.1% but apparently are not incorporated into correctness. Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632/0.696 is moderate rather than compellingly high, and claims of significant superiority have no reported tests.

Claims about dataset characteristics are post-hoc and causal language is unwarranted. Two corpora simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, length, formulaicity, and semantic distribution, so the study cannot isolate which characteristic causes a workflow to perform better or show that dataset properties act independently.

The interview component lacks standard qualitative-method details, including the number interviewed, recording/transcription procedure, analysis or coding method, analyst agreement/reflexivity, and quotation-selection process. Individual interviews for asynchronous coders versus group interviews for synchronous coders introduce an additional condition confound.

Important reproducibility details remain missing despite the release claim, including the exact SBERT checkpoint, preprocessing, seeds, clustering and decoding parameters, session duration/person-hours, stopping behavior, participant-to-condition mapping, and correctness-sampling procedure. Table 10 also reverses the stated threshold: its “percentage >0.3” values correspond to the text’s percentage below 0.3.

The research question is relevant and potentially impactful, but the decisive soundness problems affect the stated central contribution. Supporting the claimed effects would require a redesigned, adequately replicated study with equal-sized collaborative groups, a genuine asynchronous consolidation workflow, and hierarchical analyses at the group/session level; this is more than a next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored NLP/HCI question: how collaborative workflow interacts with human-in-the-loop qualitative coding systems.
The empirical scope is ambitious, covering three substantially different system families, two corpora, 33 researchers, and both quantitative and qualitative evidence.

The proposed evaluation considers complementary properties—cross-codebook consistency, within-codebook cohesiveness and distinctiveness, and manual assessment of 2,400 document-theme assignments—rather than relying on a single automatic metric.
The system descriptions, prompts, complete codebooks, participant interviews, and public repository link provide useful documentation and a promising foundation for a more rigorous study.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Each asynchronous outcome is produced by one person without the stated consolidation stage, whereas each synchronous outcome is produced jointly by three people. Thus modality is confounded with team size, deliberation, total person-hours, and aggregation; the study does not establish an effect of synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration under matched resources.

There are only three asynchronous and two synchronous codebooks per system-dataset combination. Participants are reused, repeat participants always perform the asynchronous condition first, and randomization, group assignment, expertise balance, and time budgets are not reported. These design choices leave major selection, order, and learning confounds.

The significance tests are not credible as presented. Because there is only one comparison between the two synchronous codebooks, the reported t-tests necessarily appear to treat nested themes or document pairs as independent observations rather than the independently assigned coder/group units. No hierarchical analysis, effect confidence intervals, exact test statistics, or multiple-comparison correction is provided. Several differences of only 0.01 are nevertheless called significant and interpreted as substantively large.

The quality metrics have important validity limitations. Maximum theme matching permits many themes to align with one theme and does not adequately penalize unmatched themes or differing codebook cardinalities. SBERT similarity is an indirect proxy for qualitative validity, while the top-25% analysis is arbitrary and uses different selection scores across systems. The manual correctness evaluation lacks a sufficiently detailed rubric, blinding information, and uncertainty estimates, and its agreement is only moderate.

Claims about the impact of dataset characteristics are inferred from only two corpora whose size, domain, platform, length, label resources, and semantic structure all vary simultaneously. The resulting recommendations about heterogeneous versus homogeneous corpora are therefore speculative rather than identified effects.

The interview component lacks the methodological detail expected for qualitative evidence: the number of interviewees per condition, transcription and coding procedure, analyst triangulation, and treatment of individual versus group-interview effects are absent. Reproducibility is further limited by missing statistical units, session durations, embedding checkpoint, decoding settings, and random seeds; Table 10 also contradicts its surrounding text, and the identical Climate codebooks reported for the relational and LLM systems are unexplained. Overall, substantial redesign or matched-condition data and a hierarchical reanalysis are needed before the main claims meet the soundness threshold for Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-studied NLP/HCI question: how collaborative workflow affects human-in-the-loop qualitative coding.

The empirical scope is comparatively broad, covering three distinct system paradigms, two substantially different corpora, real users, and multiple quality dimensions rather than a single automated metric.
The post-hoc evaluation of 2,400 document-theme assignments, with duplicate annotation, adjudication, and reported agreement, is a useful attempt to evaluate assignment correctness directly.
The appendices expose codebooks, prompts, operational details, corpus statistics, and computational cost, while the linked repository could support further reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration. The asynchronous condition consists of single coders and apparently includes no consolidation step, whereas each synchronous condition uses a three-person team. Modality is therefore confounded with team size, deliberation, and aggregation, and the implemented asynchronous condition differs from the workflow defined in the introduction.

There are only two synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks per system-dataset cell. The reported unpaired t-tests appear to treat dependent theme- or document-level measurements as independent replicates: even differences of roughly 0.01 are labeled significant. Without analyses at the actual experimental-unit level or an appropriate hierarchical model, the significance claims constitute likely pseudoreplication. Exact p-values, degrees of freedom, confidence intervals, effect sizes, and multiple-comparison correction are also absent.

Participant assignment is insufficiently controlled and documented. Participants vary widely in expertise, some appear in multiple experiments, asynchronous participation always precedes synchronous participation, and neither randomization nor condition balance is reported. Session duration, effort, and exposure to documents are also uncontrolled or unspecified.

The proposed consistency metric uses maximum, apparently many-to-one theme matching. It does not clearly penalize unmatched themes, is sensitive to codebook size, and may be asymmetric. Because theme counts differ considerably across conditions, this can bias comparisons. High SBERT centroid similarity—especially on a homogeneous corpus—is also not evidence that two qualitative themes have equivalent meanings; the framework lacks construct validation against expert judgments.

The correctness analysis lacks uncertainty estimates and a reported statistical test despite claims that some conditions “significantly” outperform others. Sampling 200 items per broad condition leaves unclear how samples are distributed across codebooks and themes, whether evaluators were blinded, and whether the LLM's substantial invalid/unlabeled output rate (up to 16.1%) is included. Moderate annotation agreement further warrants uncertainty analysis.

Claims about effects of corpus characteristics are post-hoc and unsupported by only two datasets, whose domain, platform, size, document length, and auxiliary annotations all vary together. Table 10 also labels the 14.14/62.55 values as percentages above 0.3, whereas the prose interprets them as percentages below 0.3; the latter is the direction consistent with the other statistics.

The qualitative user study is under-specified: the number interviewed per condition, recording/transcription procedure, analysis or coding method, analyst agreement, and saturation are not reported. Individual asynchronous interviews and group synchronous interviews introduce an additional confound, so selected quotations cannot robustly support the design recommendations.

Important reproducibility details remain missing despite the repository link, including the exact SBERT checkpoint, random seeds, LLM decoding settings, climate-specific relational concepts, metric aggregation formulas, statistical units, and participant-to-condition assignments. The identical climate codebooks reported for the relational and LLM systems also require an explanation of whether codebooks were reused or experiments were paired.

Overall, the topic and collected data are promising, but the current design and inferential analysis do not support the paper's central collaboration-effect claims. A viable resubmission would need substantial reanalysis and narrower exploratory claims, or additional randomized and replicated group-level experiments with a genuine asynchronous-collaboration condition.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-studied question at the intersection of NLP, HCI, and qualitative research: how collaborative workflows interact with NLP-assisted theme discovery.
The empirical effort is ambitious, covering three substantially different computational approaches, two corpora, 33 researchers, and a manual audit of 2,400 document-theme assignments.

The proposed evaluation considers complementary properties—cross-codebook consistency, within-codebook cohesion/distinctiveness, and assignment correctness—rather than relying on a single topic-coherence measure.

The correctness audit uses multiple annotators, adjudication, and reported Krippendorff's alpha. The appendices provide codebooks, prompts, several hyperparameters, and corpus analyses, while a public code/data repository is linked.
The presentation is generally clear, and the mixed results across systems and datasets are potentially useful for designing future human-in-the-loop tools.
weaknesses: The principal comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Synchronous conditions use teams of three, whereas asynchronous conditions appear to use one coder without the consolidation step included in the paper's own definition of asynchronous collaboration. Coder count, person-hours, deliberation, and consolidation are therefore confounded with synchrony, so the central causal claim is not supported.

There are only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per dataset-system cell. The manuscript does not identify the observational unit used in its unpaired t-tests; treating themes or document pairs as independent would be severe pseudoreplication, while valid group-level tests would have only two versus three observations. Repeated participants, lack of reported randomization or balancing, many uncorrected comparisons, and absent exact p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes further undermine the significance claims. Differences as small as 0.01 are labeled significant and then described as substantively meaningful.

The dataset analysis cannot establish effects of dataset characteristics: there is only one corpus at each point, and topic, platform, size, document length, formulaicity, and semantic diversity all vary together. Explanations attributing outcomes to particular characteristics are post-hoc hypotheses, not independently supported findings.

The proposed metrics need stronger validation. Maximum many-to-one theme matching can ignore unmatched themes and split/merge errors and is sensitive to codebook size, which ranges from 7 to 25 themes. Embedding-based cohesion is also confounded by theme granularity and corpus geometry and is not demonstrated to correspond to qualitative validity. No random or noninteractive baselines, alternative embeddings, or sensitivity analyses are provided.

The correctness evaluation is insufficiently specified: the paper plots F1 without defining its construction from judged document-theme pairs, does not explain blinding or aggregation across codebooks, and provides no uncertainty or statistical test despite claiming significant superiority. Uniform sampling across themes and quartiles also does not estimate corpus-level assignment accuracy without appropriate weighting.

The LLM condition has Gwet's AC1 values of only 0.25–0.62 and leaves 0.7%–16.1% of documents unlabeled, but the treatment of these failures in the reported metrics is unexplained. Prompt selection lacks a held-out evaluation, and decoding settings are missing. Moreover, participant accounting is internally unclear: the stated design implies 36 synchronous participant slots, although 33 participants reportedly completed at most one synchronous experiment; verbatim-identical relational and LLM codebooks in the climate condition further require an explicit account of reuse and statistical dependence.

The interview component is reported as selected observations and quotations without a qualitative analysis protocol, coder agreement, prevalence counts, negative cases, or condition-level participant counts. Synchronous participants were interviewed in groups while asynchronous participants were interviewed individually, introducing another modality confound.

These concerns affect the validity of the central conclusions rather than merely presentation. A viable resubmission should either run a controlled, sufficiently replicated comparison with matched teams and actual asynchronous consolidation, or reframe the work as an exploratory descriptive study and substantially revise the statistical analysis and claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored NLP/HCI question: how collaborative workflows interact with human-in-the-loop qualitative coding systems. Comparing topic-model, relational, and LLM-based approaches on two real-world corpora is relevant to computational linguistics.

The empirical effort is substantial: 33 researchers, 30 reported sessions, complete codebooks, multiple quantitative perspectives, 2,400 manually evaluated document-theme pairs, and post-session interviews. Reporting system- and corpus-dependent outcomes is more informative than presenting a single aggregate leaderboard.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. It links a public repository and provides useful appendices containing prompts, system operations, model settings, dataset statistics, and session-level codebooks.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Asynchronous outcomes are produced by one coder, with no reported consolidation stage, whereas synchronous outcomes are produced by three-coder teams. Communication is therefore bundled with team size and potentially three times the labor; session duration and person-hours are not controlled. Participant allocation and expertise balancing are also unspecified, while reused participants always performed asynchronous work first. Consequently, the claimed effect of synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration is not identifiable from this design.

The statistical inference is not credible at the treatment level. Each system-dataset cell contains only three asynchronous and two synchronous codebooks, and pairwise consistency comparisons reuse the same codebooks. Nevertheless, unpaired t-tests apparently treat nested themes, documents, or document pairs as independent observations. The paper gives neither statistical sample units nor exact p-values, confidence intervals, hierarchical analyses, or multiple-comparison correction. Table 2 even marks differences of approximately 0.01 as significant and describes them as substantial. This pseudoreplication directly undermines the main claims.

Several proposed metrics have unresolved construct-validity problems. Maximum best-match alignment permits many-to-one matches, does not clearly specify direction or symmetrization, and is biased by codebook size, which ranges from 7 to 25 themes. SBERT similarity rewards embedding-space topical compactness, which is not necessarily equivalent to the validity of an interpretive qualitative theme; the same representation also contributes to system initialization or propagation, creating circularity. The arbitrary top-25-percent analysis and near-saturated centroid similarities are not validated against human judgments of codebook quality.

Claims about dataset characteristics and intervention richness substantially exceed the evidence. The two corpora simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, document length, formulaicity, semantic diversity, and available auxiliary labels, so none of these factors has an independently estimated effect. Likewise, one implementation represents each methodological category. Recommendations assigning collaboration modes to corpus types, and the claim that richer intervention mechanisms benefit more from synchronous discussion, are therefore post-hoc hypotheses rather than supported conclusions.

The correctness and interview evaluations are insufficiently specified. Figure 4 reports F1 although the paper does not explain how precision and recall arise from judgments of already-assigned document-theme pairs, how samples are divided among codebooks, whether evaluators are blinded, or whether differences are statistically reliable. For the interviews, the number interviewed, recording/transcription procedure, qualitative analysis method, coders, and prevalence or negative evidence for reported themes are absent; individual asynchronous interviews and group synchronous interviews further confound the comparison.

Reproducibility is only partial despite the linked artifacts. Important details such as exact embedding checkpoints, preprocessing, random seeds, decoding parameters, aggregation units, and matching procedures are missing from the manuscript. The Climate relational and LLM appendices contain identical codebooks without explaining whether sessions or inputs were reused, making independence and the reported experiment count unclear. Table 10 labels percentages as similarity greater than 0.3 while the prose interprets the same values as below 0.3. Addressing the decisive design and inference problems would require substantial new balanced experimentation, not merely clarification or reanalysis.

strengths: Addresses an important CL/HCI question and undertakes an ambitious study spanning 30 sessions, 33 researchers, three different NLP-assisted coding approaches, and two real-world corpora. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ev6ox4wl/call-09907f7794ad41c9a2df3e5e9c87a8d2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Triangulates document-overlap and embedding-based measures with 2,400 manually judged assignments and participant interviews instead of relying on a single automatic metric. The use of two annotators, tie-breaking adjudication, and reported Krippendorff's alpha is welcome.

Uses common starting configurations within each system and reports all resulting codebook names, prompt templates, system operations, corpus analyses, and approximate LLM compute requirements in appendices.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and relevant to researchers developing human-in-the-loop NLP tools for qualitative analysis.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Each synchronous output is produced jointly by three people, whereas each asynchronous output is produced by one person working alone; the stated asynchronous consolidation never occurs. Person-hours and session duration are not controlled, participant assignment is not reported as randomized or matched, and reused participants always complete asynchronous work first. Team size, labor, coder identity and expertise, practice effects, and synchrony are therefore inseparable.

There are only two independent synchronous groups and three independent asynchronous coders per system-dataset cell. The paper does not state the sample or unit used in its t-tests, but the reported standard deviations and significance tests appear to treat nested themes or document similarities as independent observations. Because modality is assigned at the session/group level, this is pseudoreplication; repeated participants add further dependence. Exact p-values, degrees of freedom, confidence intervals, effect sizes, power analysis, and multiple-comparison correction are absent, while tiny differences such as 0.44 versus 0.43 are characterized as significant and substantively large.

The consistency metric is insufficiently specified and potentially biased. Maximum matching appears to permit many-to-one alignments, is not clearly symmetrized, and does not penalize unmatched themes. Since codebooks contain between 7 and 25 themes, the score is sensitive to granularity and chance maxima. No random or corpus-level baseline and no human validation are supplied; centroid similarities near 0.94-0.98 may mainly reflect corpus homogeneity.

Embedding cohesion and separation are not established as valid measures of qualitative thematic quality. The relational system itself clusters and propagates labels using SBERT, which is then also used to evaluate cohesion and semantic consistency, creating circularity in cross-system comparisons. The systems also use different notions of confidence to select their top quartiles.

The correctness evaluation is not reproducible from the description. It reports F1 without defining the prediction and gold-label construction, negative cases, recall denominator, or aggregation procedure. Rater instructions, blinding, and independence from the original sessions are unspecified, and Figure 4 lacks uncertainty intervals. LLM runs leave up to 16.1% of documents unlabeled through invalid generated labels, but coverage and the treatment of these omissions are not incorporated into quality comparisons; remaining unmapped documents from the relational system are likewise not reported.

Claims that particular dataset characteristics independently determine the preferable workflow, and that systems with richer intervention benefit more from synchrony, are post-hoc generalizations from only two datasets and one system per category, with all dataset and system attributes covarying. A manual-coding control is also absent. Table 10 additionally labels the 14.14/62.55 values as percentages above 0.3, whereas the text interprets them as percentages below 0.3.

The interview component does not report the number of interviews, recording or transcription procedure, qualitative analysis method, coders, saturation, or treatment of negative cases. Individual interviews for asynchronous participants and group interviews for synchronous participants introduce another modality confound, so the qualitative claims and design recommendations have weak evidential grounding.

Although a public repository is a strength, key reproducibility details remain missing, including participant-to-condition allocation, time budgets, full theme definitions, evaluation sampling and annotation instructions, statistical specifications, embedding/model revisions, LLM decoding parameters and seeds, and repeated stochastic runs. Supporting the stated causal and general claims would require a redesigned, adequately replicated and counterbalanced study rather than a minor revision.
