strengths: The paper addresses a practically important, ACL-relevant question: how collaborative workflow interacts with NLP-assisted qualitative coding.

The empirical scope is substantial: 33 participants, three technically different systems, two contrasting datasets, 30 reported sessions, controlled initial partitions, and a manual audit of 2,400 document-theme assignments.

The evaluation considers overlap, semantic structure, human-judged assignment correctness, and participant experience rather than relying on one automatic metric. Double annotation, tie-breaking, and agreement reporting are welcome.

The manuscript is clearly organized and provides prompts, codebook lists, dataset diagnostics, and a public artifact link, facilitating scrutiny. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-jt3f7pd0/call-175b9fda148a4fb995d5dd93ba6c992f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central claim about collaboration modality is not identified by the design. Each asynchronous output is produced by one coder, apparently without the promised consolidation stage, whereas each synchronous output is produced by three coders deliberating together. Modality is therefore confounded with team size, labor, interaction, and aggregation. The experiment supports at most a comparison of solo coders with synchronous teams, not synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration.

There are only three asynchronous and two synchronous codebooks per system-dataset combination. The unpaired t-tests appear to treat themes or document-pair similarities as independent observations despite their nesting within five codebooks and reuse of the same documents. Table 2 even marks rounded differences of 0.00–0.01 as significant. The paper gives no test units, exact p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, hierarchical analysis, or multiple-comparison correction. Consequently, the reported significance cannot substantiate general modality effects.

Participant assignment and exposure are insufficiently controlled. Thirty sessions imply repeated participation among the 33 researchers, but assignments and overlaps are not reported. Repeat participants always completed asynchronous work first, creating a possible practice or dataset-familiarity advantage for later synchronous work. Expertise, person-hours, session duration, group composition, and subjective stopping criteria are also not balanced or modeled.

The proposed metrics lack construct validation as measures of qualitative-analysis quality. Embedding cohesion or separation does not by itself establish that a theme is insightful, valid, complete, or useful. Maximum many-to-one theme matching is sensitive to codebook size and granularity, need not penalize missing themes, and may be asymmetric. Selecting the closest 25% of documents mechanically improves cohesion. Claims about 'deeper' or 'clearer' analysis therefore exceed the evidence.

SBERT is both part of the relational pipeline and the principal semantic evaluator, potentially favoring outputs organized in that representation. No alternative encoders, human semantic alignment, random baselines, or robustness analyses are provided.

Claims that particular dataset characteristics independently determine performance are unsupported by only two corpora. Domain, platform, size, document length, available auxiliary labels, formulaicity, and semantic diversity all change simultaneously; the post-hoc diagnostics cannot isolate any of them or justify modality-selection recommendations.

The correctness study is promising but underreported. It is unclear how samples are distributed across individual codebooks, whether evaluators were independent and blinded, what theme definitions they saw, and how differing unmapped rates were handled. Agreement is only moderate, while exact scores, uncertainty, and statistical comparisons are absent. LLM agreement used for prompt selection is low (0.25–0.62), prompts are selected on the same human-labeled examples rather than held-out data, and up to 16.1% of outputs use nonexistent labels.

The climate codebooks in Tables 15 and 16 are verbatim identical for the relational and LLM conditions across all five sessions. This strongly suggests shared or reused human outputs, which would make those systems non-independent evidence; the experimental relationship is not explained. More broadly, the exact SBERT checkpoint, random seeds, selected prompt per codebook, LLM decoding settings, participant allocations, and analysis code for the statistical tests are not specified in the paper.

The interview component does not report the number interviewed, analysis procedure, coding reliability, or prevalence of themes. Moreover, synchronous participants were interviewed in groups while asynchronous participants were interviewed individually. A few selected quotations cannot support the broad user-study conclusions.

These problems affect the study's core inference and cannot be repaired through clearer writing alone. A convincing resubmission needs matched synchronous and asynchronous teams, an explicit asynchronous consolidation protocol, counterbalancing, substantially more independent group-level replications, and inference at the group level. This likely requires a major new study rather than a next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored question at the intersection of NLP, HCI, and qualitative research, with clear practical motivation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-il5do4dy/call-4723230b936c498581ce10116ee4081d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical effort is unusually broad: 30 sessions with 33 researchers, three substantially different NLP-assisted systems, and two real-world corpora.

The evaluation considers complementary views of output quality and includes 2,400 manually assessed document-theme pairs, duplicate annotation with adjudication, reported Krippendorff alpha, interviews, and extensive codebook appendices.
The presentation is generally clear, and the paper transparently reports prompt templates, LLM agreement and non-coverage rates, computational cost, corpus statistics, and a public code/data link.
weaknesses: The decisive construct-validity problem is that synchronous three-person teams are compared with single asynchronous coders. The asynchronous condition includes no team consolidation despite the paper's own definition of asynchronous collaboration. Collaboration timing is therefore confounded with group size, number of perspectives, and total human effort, so the central claimed effect cannot be attributed to synchronicity.

There are only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per system-dataset cell. Participants repeat across experiments and always perform asynchronous work first, introducing dependence and order effects. The unpaired t-tests apparently treat nested themes or document similarities as independent observations rather than treating sessions as the experimental units; the test samples and degrees of freedom are not reported, and numerous comparisons receive no multiplicity correction. Consequently, the significance claims are not supported.

The proposed metrics have not been validated as measures of qualitative-analysis quality. Maximum theme matching permits many-to-one alignments and is sensitive to codebook size, which ranges from 7 to 25 themes. SBERT similarity partly reuses the representation employed by the systems, while centroid-based top-quartile selection and intra-theme similarity reward finer semantic partitions. These measures do not establish interpretive usefulness, theme completeness, or correctness of the codebook itself.

The correctness study lacks per-condition numerical results, uncertainty intervals, test details, rater blinding, and a sufficiently specified judgment rubric. It is also unclear whether unmapped outputs are penalized; this matters because the LLM leaves up to 16.1% of documents unlabeled. Selecting prompts on the same human-labeled examples used to measure agreement, without held-out validation, further biases that component.

Claims that particular corpus characteristics cause the observed differences are post-hoc and cannot be isolated from only two datasets that vary simultaneously in domain, size, genre, source, and length. Table 10 also labels the 14.14/62.55 row as similarity greater than 0.3, whereas the prose describes these values as similarity below 0.3; the table as written contradicts the claimed homogeneity pattern.

The interview component does not report how many interviews were analyzed, a qualitative coding procedure, coder reliability or reflexivity, theme prevalence, or saturation. Group interviews for synchronous participants and individual interviews for asynchronous participants create an additional reporting confound, and some questions are leading.

Important reproducibility details are absent from the manuscript, including participant-to-session assignment, randomization, session durations and person-hours, the exact SBERT checkpoint, clustering seeds, relational thresholds, LLM decoding settings, and the statistical analysis unit. Addressing the central claims requires a controlled, adequately replicated study with equal-sized teams in both modalities, not merely presentational revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored NLP/HCI question: how collaboration practices interact with human-in-the-loop qualitative coding systems. The manuscript reviewed is :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-_1ijn_pr/call-10b46931184c466abe16276ffc08f098/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The empirical effort is substantial: 33 researchers, three distinct system families, two corpora, 30 reported experiments, and a 2,400-pair post-hoc correctness annotation.
Considering consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, correctness, and user experience together is more informative than evaluating an interactive system using a single automatic metric.

The paper is clearly organized and unusually transparent about final codebooks, LLM prompts, compute requirements, model–human agreement, and rates of invalid LLM labels. Public code and experimental outputs further support reproducibility.
The results usefully demonstrate strong system- and corpus-dependent variation, even though the present design cannot support the paper's stronger causal explanations.
weaknesses: The decisive soundness problem is the effective sample size. Each dataset–system condition has only two independent synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks. The reported t-tests apparently treat themes or document similarities nested within those codebooks as independent observations; effects as small as 0.01 consequently become significant. This is pseudoreplication unless a hierarchical or cluster-aware analysis establishes otherwise. No multiple-testing correction, group-level confidence intervals, or suitably powered replication is provided.

Collaboration modality is confounded with team size and labor: a synchronous output is created by three people, whereas an asynchronous output is created by one person and undergoes no reported consolidation, despite asynchronous collaboration being defined as independent coding followed by consolidation. Participant reuse, non-random assignment, and the rule that repeated participants always perform asynchronous work first add unmodeled identity, expertise, and order effects. The study therefore compares three-person teams with solo coders, not synchronous with asynchronous collaboration cleanly.

Several proposed quality measures have weak construct validity. Maximum many-to-one theme matching is sensitive to codebook size and lacks a symmetric one-to-one or chance baseline. High intra-theme relative to inter-theme SBERT similarity does not by itself establish qualitative validity or distinctiveness. Moreover, the relational system is built with SBERT while several evaluation measures use the same representation, creating a circular advantage. The framework is not validated against expert judgments of overall codebook quality.

The correctness study is insufficiently specified. The paper calls it manual checking of assigned document–theme pairs, but Figure 4 reports F1 without defining the classification task, negatives, or aggregation. It omits per-codebook sample allocation, annotator expertise and blinding, decision guidelines, confidence intervals, and a statistical test supporting claims such as significant outperformance. Moderate Krippendorff alpha supports annotation reliability, not the correctness of an inherently inductive theme system.

Claims about dataset characteristics and intervention richness are post-hoc and causal in tone. With only two corpora that differ simultaneously in domain, platform, size, length, auxiliary labels, formulaicity, and semantics, no individual characteristic can be isolated. Likewise, one system per broad methodological family cannot establish that richer intervention mechanisms cause greater benefits from synchronous work.

The relationship between experiments is unclear. Tables 15 and 16 contain exactly the same five climate codebooks for the relational and LLM systems. If codebooks or sessions were reused, system-level observations are dependent and the comparison concerns propagation rather than full theme discovery; if they were independently produced, the exact identity requires explanation. This ambiguity also affects the claimed total of 30 experiments.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the artifact release: the manuscript omits the exact SBERT checkpoint, key clustering and random-seed details, session time budgets, participant-to-condition allocation, LLM decoding parameters, and how invalid/unlabeled LLM outputs—up to 16.1%—enter each metric. Table 10 also labels values as percentages above 0.3 while the prose interprets them as percentages below 0.3.

The interview evidence cannot substantiate the stated design recommendations. The number of interviews, recording/transcription procedure, qualitative analysis method, coder agreement, and prevalence of reported themes are absent; individual asynchronous interviews and synchronous group interviews also create different disclosure and conformity conditions.

Overall, this is a valuable exploratory dataset and case study, but the invalid or undocumented inferential analysis and major condition confounds prevent a Findings-level soundness recommendation. A revision should either add independently replicated, balanced conditions with cluster-aware statistics or sharply narrow the paper to descriptive observations and validate the proposed metrics.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored NLP/HCI question: how human collaboration interacts with NLP-assisted qualitative coding. Comparing three system paradigms and two substantially different corpora is ambitious and relevant.
The study represents considerable empirical effort, involving 33 researchers, 30 reported experimental configurations, a 2,400-item post-hoc correctness assessment, and participant interviews.

The proposed evaluation examines consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness rather than relying on a single topic-coherence measure. Reporting annotator agreement and mixed correctness results is also valuable.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, provides extensive appendices with prompts and resulting codebooks, and links public code and experimental data.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Each asynchronous outcome is produced by one person, whereas each synchronous outcome is produced by a three-person team; the stated asynchronous consolidation step is not actually evaluated. Team size, total person-effort, discussion, and modality are therefore inseparable, so the evidence cannot support causal claims about synchrony versus asynchrony.

There are only three asynchronous individuals and two synchronous groups per system-dataset cell. The reported unpaired t-tests apparently treat themes, document pairs, or other nested observations as independent: with only one synchronous codebook-pair for consistency and two synchronous experimental units otherwise, the many significance findings—including differences of 0.01—cannot plausibly reflect valid group-level inference. Units of analysis, exact tests, confidence intervals, effect sizes, power, and multiple-comparison correction are missing.

Participant allocation is insufficiently controlled. Some participants occur in multiple experiments and always complete asynchronous work first, creating learning and carryover into synchronous sessions; randomization, condition balance, expertise balance, time-on-task, and participant/session mappings are not reported.

The proposed metrics are not adequately validated as measures of qualitative-analysis quality. Maximum-over-theme matching is many-to-one and biased by unequal codebook sizes; raw SBERT similarities may conflate corpus-wide similarity with theme quality; and using SBERT both inside the relational system and for evaluation creates circularity. Agreement and embedding cohesion are not necessarily equivalent to interpretive validity, completeness, or usefulness.

The conclusions substantially exceed the mixed descriptive evidence. Consistency often differs little across modalities and favors asynchronous coding on Climate Jaccard scores; cohesion advantages are frequently only 0.01; and correctness changes direction across tools and datasets. Claims that synchronous collaboration enables deeper analysis, that richer intervention mechanisms benefit more from it, or that particular dataset properties determine the preferred protocol are therefore not established.

The two datasets differ simultaneously in domain, size, document length, formulaicity, auxiliary annotations, and semantic distribution, so individual dataset characteristics cannot be identified as causes. Some supporting analyses are underspecified, and Table 10 labels the 14.14/62.55 row as similarity greater than 0.3 while the prose describes those values as similarity below 0.3.

The correctness study omits condition-level uncertainty, statistical tests, evaluator blinding, detailed guidelines, and handling of the LLM's 0.7–16.1% invalid labels. The interview component reports neither its participant count nor a transcription/coding procedure, saturation analysis, theme frequencies, or negative cases; individual versus group interviewing introduces another modality confound.

Paper-level reproducibility remains incomplete despite the repository link: the SBERT checkpoint, assignment thresholds, seeds, decoding settings, selected prompt per codebook, full codebook definitions, session durations, and interaction logs are not specified. The exact duplication of all Climate relational and LLM codebooks is also unexplained, leaving unclear whether these were independent experiments or reused human outputs.

Correcting the statistical analysis alone would leave too few independent experimental units, while resolving the primary confound requires matched asynchronous teams, controlled effort, randomized or counterbalanced assignment, and substantially more group-level replications. This amounts to a major new study rather than a next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored question at the intersection of NLP, HCI, and qualitative research: how collaboration affects NLP-assisted theme discovery. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xe5rxyea/call-92c58737c948494ab8826a1d682a0331/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical effort is substantial: 33 researchers, 30 coding sessions, three distinct system paradigms, two corpora, and 2,400 post-hoc document-theme judgments.

Evaluating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and correctness is preferable to relying on a single automatic topic-quality measure. The comparison of lexical overlap, embedding-based measures, and human judgments is conceptually useful.

The paper reports appropriately mixed results rather than presenting one universally superior system, and the observations concerning user control and deliberation could inform future interactive-system design.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with public code/data, prompt templates, complete codebook lists, computational-cost information, and useful dataset analyses.
weaknesses: The central treatment is not collaboration modality alone. Each asynchronous output is produced by one coder without the consolidation stage used in the paper's own definition of asynchronous collaboration, whereas each synchronous output is produced by three coders jointly. Modality is therefore confounded with team size, person-hours, deliberation, and consensus construction. Session duration, expertise balance, and randomized assignment are not reported. Some participants also complete multiple sessions, always asynchronous first, creating a possible experience/order effect. Consequently, the study supports an exploratory comparison of solo coding and synchronous teams, not a causal claim about synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration.

There are only two synchronous and three asynchronous independent codebooks per system-dataset cell. The unit of analysis for the unpaired t-tests is not specified; significance apparently relies on nested theme- or document-level similarities even though those observations share codebooks and documents. Such pseudoreplication cannot replace inference over independent teams. Numerous tests are conducted without multiplicity correction, exact p-values, confidence intervals, or effect sizes, and differences as small as 0.01 are described as significant or markedly better.

The consistency metric uses directional, many-to-one maximum matching, which can inflate agreement, ignore unmatched themes, and favor codebooks with more themes. Theme counts vary considerably, yet this is not controlled. A bijective matching analysis, unmatched-theme penalty, null baseline, and sensitivity analysis are needed.

The embedding-based evaluation has circularity and construct-validity problems: SBERT helps form or propagate relational-system assignments and then evaluates their semantic quality. The top-25% analysis selects central documents by system-specific scores, mechanically increasing cohesion. No evidence establishes that these proxy metrics correspond to expert judgments of qualitatively useful themes, and centroid similarity is nearly saturated.

The correctness evaluation is insufficiently specified. It is unclear how 200 examples are allocated across sessions, themes, and quartiles; how annotators were trained or blinded; and how F1 is computed from checks of predicted document-theme pairs, which as described do not reveal false negatives. Figure 4 lacks uncertainty estimates. Moreover, the LLM leaves up to 16.1% of documents unlabeled, but the treatment of these failures is unexplained and may make assigned-only correctness and cohesion estimates optimistic.

Claims about dataset characteristics are based on only two corpora that simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, length, supervision, and formulaicity; these factors cannot be independently attributed. Table 10 labels a statistic as similarity greater than 0.3 while the text interprets the same values as below 0.3. The claim of high thematic clarity from fitted GMM posterior confidence is also not well justified, particularly given silhouette scores near zero.

The interview component lacks the sample size and condition breakdown, recording/transcription procedure, coding method, analyst agreement, saturation criterion, and prevalence of themes. Individual interviews for solo coders versus group interviews for synchronous teams introduce another confound, so the few quotations cannot substantiate the stated user-study findings.

Despite the public repository, important reproducibility details are absent from the paper, including the SBERT checkpoint, preprocessing and random seeds, clustering/GMM/DBSCAN settings, LLM decoding and malformed-output handling, prompt-selection protocol, participant-to-session allocation, and standardized stopping or time rules.

The conclusions overstate the evidence: one implementation cannot represent an entire methodological category, two datasets cannot establish corpus-level moderators, and mixed correctness results do not support broad claims that collaboration modality significantly improves output quality. Addressing the original claims would require a balanced asynchronous-team condition, more independent teams, and group-level statistical analysis; otherwise the paper should be substantially reframed as a descriptive pilot study.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, underexplored NLP/HCI question: how collaborative workflows interact with NLP-assisted qualitative coding. It is clearly relevant to computational linguistics. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-e6ptmxux/call-26f0c59e3f994610b8d82d085af86610/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical effort is substantial: 33 researchers, three distinct system paradigms, two contrasting real-world corpora, complete induced codebooks, and post-hoc human evaluation of 2,400 document-theme assignments.

The evaluation usefully triangulates document overlap, embedding-based cohesion and distinctiveness, human correctness judgments, and participant interviews. The paper also reports mixed, context-dependent outcomes rather than forcing a single system or workflow to appear universally superior.

A public code/data repository, model and topic-model configurations, prompt templates, human-model agreement, unlabeled-document rates, corpus analyses, and verbatim codebooks provide useful reproducibility support.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. A synchronous output is produced by a three-person team, whereas each asynchronous output is produced by one person and is never consolidated with the other asynchronous coders' work. Thus team size, deliberation, aggregate labor, and modality are confounded; the study supports at most a comparison of synchronous teams with solo coding, not the claimed effect of synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration.

The inferential statistics are not valid at the treatment level. Each system-dataset condition has only two synchronous teams and three asynchronous individuals. A synchronous condition therefore supplies only one between-codebook consistency comparison, yet Tables 1 and 2 report standard deviations and unpaired t-tests over nested theme- or document-level observations. Treating these as independent is pseudoreplication. Participant reuse, the fixed asynchronous-first order, heterogeneous expertise, and the absence of multiplicity correction across dozens of tests further undermine the significance claims.

The proposed framework is insufficiently validated as a measure of qualitative-analysis quality. Maximum best-theme matching permits many-to-one alignments, may be asymmetric, and favors codebooks with more candidate themes; observed codebook sizes range from 7 to 25 themes. SBERT is also used both to construct parts of the relational/LLM pipelines and to evaluate semantic quality, making the evidence partly circular. High embedding compactness does not by itself establish interpretive validity.

The correctness evaluation is materially underspecified. The paper does not explain allocation across codebooks and themes, evaluator blinding, or the detailed judgment protocol. More importantly, evaluating sampled assigned document-theme pairs appears to yield correctness/precision judgments, but the manuscript does not explain how false negatives required for the reported F1 scores are obtained. Figure 4 supplies no uncertainty intervals or documented tests despite claims of significant superiority.

Claims about dataset characteristics are causal overinterpretations of two observational cases. Domain, platform, corpus size, document length, formulaicity, semantic diversity, available auxiliary concepts, and sampling proportion all vary together. The study cannot identify which property caused a workflow difference, and several supposedly strong cohesion effects are only 0.01 in absolute similarity.

The interview component lacks basic qualitative-method details: participant counts by condition, duration, transcription, coding procedure, analyst roles, agreement or reflexivity, and saturation are unreported. Synchronous participants were interviewed in groups while asynchronous participants were interviewed individually, introducing another modality confound, and the conclusions rely mainly on a few illustrative quotations.

Important reproducibility ambiguities remain despite the repository: session duration/person-hours, participant-to-condition assignment, random seeds, exact SBERT checkpoint, LLM decoding parameters, and handling of invalid or unlabeled LLM outputs are missing. Moreover, the relational and LLM Climate codebooks in Tables 15 and 16 are verbatim identical despite being described as separate experiments, which requires an explanation of reuse, independence, or a possible reporting error.

These problems directly affect the paper's central claims and preclude a Findings recommendation. A viable resubmission would need either a matched, adequately replicated team design with hierarchical inference or a substantially narrower descriptive framing, corrected analyses, and much more cautious conclusions.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, underexplored question about how collaboration shapes NLP-assisted qualitative analysis and is clearly relevant to human-centered NLP. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-nbbdk8sn/call-f06352ab5cd54cc88f50cfd538ed0620/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical effort is substantial: three interactive paradigms, two corpora, 33 researchers, 30 reported experiments, and a manual audit of 2,400 document-theme assignments.

The evaluation usefully separates overlap-based consistency, semantic similarity, within-codebook cohesion/distinctiveness, and assignment correctness. Reporting low LLM agreement and unlabeled-document rates is commendably transparent.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with helpful diagrams and extensive appendices containing prompts, codebooks, operational details, and corpus analyses. A public code/data release is also stated.
weaknesses: The central treatment is not isolated. The asynchronous condition uses individual coders without the promised consolidation, whereas the synchronous condition uses three-coder teams. Consequently, synchronicity is confounded with coder count, discussion, aggregation, and likely total human effort. Repeated participation, a fixed asynchronous-first order, unspecified condition assignment, and unreported time-on-task add further confounds. The study therefore cannot support causal claims about the effects of collaboration modality.

There are only two synchronous group-level replicates and three asynchronous coder-level replicates per system-dataset combination. The statistical unit is not defined; the reported unpaired t-tests appear to rely on nested theme- or document-level observations, which would be pseudoreplication because modality is assigned at the session/group level. The analysis also lacks multiplicity correction, exact p-values, confidence intervals, and an appropriate clustered or repeated-measures model. Labeling p approximately 0.05 as near-significant further weakens the evidence. Thus the main significance claims are not supported.

The proposed metrics have unresolved construct-validity problems. Maximum many-to-one theme matching can reward broad or duplicated themes, is sensitive to codebook size, and is not clearly symmetrized or chance-corrected. SBERT centroid scores are nearly saturated, the exact encoder is unspecified, and semantic cluster separation is not necessarily equivalent to qualitative analytic quality because valid themes may overlap. The system-specific definition of the top 25% also limits cross-system comparability, and the metric suite is not validated against expert judgments of codebook quality.

Claims about dataset characteristics are overextended. With only two corpora that simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, document length, formulaicity, and auxiliary annotations, none of these factors can be identified independently. Likewise, one implementation per loosely defined system category cannot establish conclusions about topic-model, relational, or LLM approaches generally. The resulting workflow recommendations are plausible hypotheses rather than demonstrated findings.

The correctness study omits important details about sample allocation, evaluator expertise, annotation criteria, blinding, and dependence among judgments; Figure 4 provides no uncertainty, yet the text asserts significant differences without reporting a test. The qualitative study similarly lacks interview sample counts, recording/transcription procedures, a coding method, analyst agreement or reflexivity, and systematic evidence beyond selected quotations.

Reproducibility and reporting remain incomplete despite the stated release: key seeds, exact SBERT checkpoint, clustering settings, LLM decoding parameters/model revision, assignment rules, statistical test inputs, and participant allocation are absent. Tables 15 and 16 contain verbatim-identical Climate codebooks for supposedly separate relational and LLM experiments without explanation, while Table 10's greater-than-0.3 row contradicts both its averages and the prose. These central design and inference issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation; substantial reanalysis, claim narrowing, and likely additional controlled group-level data are needed.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important ACL-relevant question: how collaboration interacts with NLP-assisted qualitative coding. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-3o1pqn1o/call-fbd940c0c9734f20af3e16e0f06e3998/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical effort is substantial, spanning three distinct system paradigms, two sizable corpora, 33 participants, and a post-hoc audit of 2,400 document–theme pairs.

Evaluating consistency, cohesion, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness is more informative than relying on a single topic-coherence measure. The appendices provide prompts, codebooks, theme counts, and LLM agreement and failure rates.
The paper is generally readable and usefully reports mixed outcomes rather than claiming that one tool or collaboration mode always wins.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. A synchronous condition is a three-person team, whereas an asynchronous condition is one individual whose output is never consolidated. Thus modality is confounded with team size, pooled expertise, discussion, and likely total labor; moreover, the study does not actually evaluate the asynchronous collaborative workflow it defines.

There are only two synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks per system–dataset cell—the relevant independent experimental units. The analysis unit for the unpaired t-tests is not disclosed, and significance for differences as small as 0.01 strongly suggests that dependent themes or document pairs were treated as independent observations. Repeated participants, fixed asynchronous-first ordering, absent randomization details, many comparisons without correction, and no exact p-values, confidence intervals, or effect sizes further invalidate the inferential claims.

The proposed metrics have serious construct-validity problems. Maximum theme matching is many-to-one, apparently unsymmetrized, and sensitive to codebook size, which ranges from 7 to 25 themes. SBERT similarities can match lexically similar but conceptually opposite themes, while centroid scores of 0.94–0.98 indicate a ceiling effect. No random-partition, human-only, or expert-reference baseline validates that higher scores mean better qualitative analysis; consistency itself is not necessarily quality.

The cohesion analysis is partly circular: SBERT representations help construct the relational partitions and then evaluate their quality, while centroid distance also selects the reported top quartile. Different systems use different ranking criteria, and scores are not normalized for corpus-wide similarity, theme size, or codebook granularity.

The correctness evaluation is insufficiently specified. The manuscript samples assigned document–theme pairs but reports F1 without defining false negatives or explaining how F1 is computed. Exact results, uncertainty, and significance tests are absent; agreement is only moderate; evaluator blinding is unspecified; and it is unclear how the LLM's 0.7–16.1% invalid/unlabeled outputs enter any metric.

Claims about dataset characteristics cannot be supported using only two corpora that simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, document length, formulaicity, and available auxiliary labels. These are post-hoc associations, not independent effects. Table 10 also labels values as percentages above 0.3 while the text interprets them as percentages below 0.3.

The interview component is not reproducible or rigorous enough to support its recommendations: it omits the number interviewed, duration, transcription and coding procedure, analyst agreement, saturation, and prevalence of themes. Individual asynchronous interviews and group synchronous interviews introduce another confound, and the supplied script specifically references only the COVID session.

Despite the public-release claim, crucial reproducibility details are missing, including participant/team allocation, prior exposure, session duration, stopping criteria, the exact SBERT checkpoint, preprocessing and random seeds, LLM decoding settings, prompt-selection splits, assignment rules, and full statistical procedures.

These issues undermine the paper's central causal and generalizable claims rather than merely limiting novelty. A sound resubmission would require substantially more independent groups, a matched asynchronous-team consolidation condition, controlled effort and order, and a hierarchical or randomization-based analysis; this is likely longer than one review cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored NLP/HCI question: how collaborative practice interacts with human-in-the-loop qualitative coding systems.
The empirical effort is substantial, covering three technically different systems, two corpora, 33 researchers, 30 coding sessions, 2,400 post-hoc assignment judgments, and participant interviews.

Evaluating consistency, semantic cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness is broader and more appropriate than relying solely on topic coherence. The appendices provide prompts, generated codebooks, system details, and dataset analyses, while code and experimental outputs are reportedly public.
The paper reports mixed results rather than forcing a universal winner, appropriately suggesting that tool and corpus properties may matter.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. The asynchronous condition consists of one person coding independently without the consolidation step used in the paper's own definition, whereas the synchronous condition uses three-person teams. Modality is therefore confounded with team size and the presence of collaboration itself. Participants can also appear in multiple experiments and always perform asynchronous work first, creating unmodeled participant, experience, and order effects. These design problems preclude the claimed causal interpretation.

There are only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system-dataset cell. Those sessions or groups are the treatment-level experimental units, yet the reported unpaired t-tests apparently rely on dependent theme- or document-pair observations. The paper does not state test sample sizes, degrees of freedom, or exact p-values, use cluster-aware or repeated-measures analyses, provide confidence intervals, or correct for numerous comparisons. Consequently, the significance claims—including significance for differences as small as 0.01—are not credible.

The proposed consistency measure uses maximum many-to-one theme matching and does not clearly specify directional symmetrization. It ignores unmatched themes and is sensitive to the number and granularity of candidate themes, which range from 7 to 25 across codebooks. Centroid similarities near 0.94-0.98 also lack a corpus or random baseline. Thus the framework can reward overbroad or highly fragmented codebooks and has not been validated as measuring qualitative-analysis quality.

Cohesiveness and distinctiveness are likewise sensitive to theme size, document coverage, and system-specific scoring. Selecting the top quartile by proximity to the same centroid later used for evaluation is partly circular. The analysis does not establish that embedding compactness corresponds to interpretive usefulness, and no expert evaluation validates the overall themes or codebooks.

The correctness study measures only whether sampled assigned documents fit their assigned theme; it does not assess missed themes, false negatives, theme importance, codebook validity, or coverage. This particularly favors the LLM condition, where up to 16.1% of documents are unlabeled and apparently excluded. The annotation rubric, evaluator blinding, sampling allocation across sessions, uncertainty estimates, and numerical scores are not adequately reported; agreement is only moderate.

System and dataset effects remain heavily confounded. The systems expose different interaction operations and potentially different human effort, with no controlled time budget. Moreover, the relational and LLM Climate conditions contain exactly the same human-created theme inventories, but their dependency is not incorporated into the analysis. With only two corpora that simultaneously differ in domain, size, length, auxiliary labels, formulaicity, and diversity, the paper cannot identify which dataset characteristic caused an observed difference or claim that such characteristics act independently.

The interview component lacks the number of interviews, participant breakdown, coding procedure, analyst agreement, saturation criterion, and systematic presentation of evidence. Individual asynchronous interviews and group synchronous interviews introduce an additional modality confound, while a few selected quotations cannot support the stated design conclusions.

Important reproducibility details remain absent despite the public repository claim, including participant-to-condition assignments and repetitions, session durations, the exact SBERT checkpoint, random seeds, decoding settings, statistical units, and several preprocessing and clustering choices. There is also an internal labeling inconsistency in Table 10 regarding pairs above versus below 0.3 similarity.

Overall, the evidence supports an exploratory description of particular solo and team sessions, not the stronger claims that collaboration modality significantly improves outcomes, enables deeper analysis, or that identified corpus properties explain the effects. Addressing the decisive concerns would require a redesigned, randomized study with genuine asynchronous teams and consolidation, substantially more independent groups, and hierarchical analysis, which is unlikely to be completed within one review cycle.

weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration. Each asynchronous codebook is produced by one coder, whereas each synchronous codebook is jointly produced by three coders; there is no asynchronous team or consolidation stage. Consequently, synchrony is confounded with group size, person-hours, expertise diversity, and consensus formation. Claims that collaboration has significant effects are therefore unsupported.

Maximum many-to-one theme matching can inflate consistency and does not clearly penalize missing or fragmented themes; its direction, symmetrization, and aggregation across three asynchronous codebooks are unspecified. The interview component lacks a stated qualitative analysis procedure, coder counts, reliability or reflexivity practices, saturation evidence, and prevalence for the reported themes. Moreover, asynchronous participants were interviewed individually while synchronous participants were interviewed as groups. Reproducibility is further limited by missing condition-level participant allocation, session durations, exact SBERT checkpoint and preprocessing, LLM decoding settings and prompt selection per codebook, and precise statistical procedures. strengths: The paper addresses a relevant, underexplored NLP/HCI question: how collaborative practice interacts with NLP-assisted qualitative coding. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-jq444d15/call-519cfebdf5c94799a3b4fc0da72c3085/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical effort is substantial, spanning three tool paradigms, two corpora, 33 participants, 30 reported sessions, 2,400 post-hoc judgments, and participant interviews.

The attempt to triangulate overlap, semantic structure, assignment correctness, and user experience is directionally valuable; reporting full codebooks also exposes meaningful qualitative variation that aggregate scores can hide.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. Named datasets and systems, prompt templates, selected hyperparameters, hardware information, and a public repository link provide a useful reproducibility foundation.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Each synchronous result is produced by three people working together, whereas each asynchronous result is produced by one person, despite asynchronous collaboration being defined as independent coding followed by consolidation. No asynchronous consolidation occurs. Modality is therefore confounded with coder count, total labor, deliberation, and aggregation; session duration and document exposure are also uncontrolled.

There are only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per dataset-system cell, with some participants reused and no adequately described randomization, matching, or counterbalancing. The sampling unit for the unpaired t-tests is unspecified. Valid inference at the group level is essentially impossible at these sample sizes, while treating themes, assignments, or document pairs as independent would be severe pseudoreplication. Repeated participation, numerous comparisons, absent multiplicity correction, vague “near significance,” and missing exact p-values/confidence intervals further undermine the reported significance claims.

The proposed metrics lack demonstrated construct validity. Maximum theme matching is non-bijective, can reuse a counterpart theme, ignores unmatched themes, and is sensitive to differing codebook sizes. Embedding similarities lack random-partition or corpus-level baselines and may conflate topical vocabulary with qualitative meaning or stance. Selecting the 25% of documents closest under related representations and then evaluating their embedding cohesiveness is partly circular and discards most system output.

The correctness evaluation is not reproducible from the description. Figure 4 reports F1, but the text only describes adjudicating sampled assigned document-theme pairs; it does not define the prediction and reference sets, negative cases, averaging, or how recall is obtained. Uncertainty and statistical tests are absent, despite claims of significant outperformance. Coverage is not evaluated jointly with correctness, even though the LLM leaves 0.7–16.1% of documents unlabeled and other systems may also leave items unmapped.

Claims about dataset characteristics are unsupported by only two corpora, which simultaneously differ in domain, platform, size, length, formulaicity, and semantic distribution. These variables cannot be disentangled, so recommendations that heterogeneous corpora benefit from asynchronous work and homogeneous corpora from synchronous work are post-hoc hypotheses rather than established findings.

The interview component lacks a qualitative analysis method: there is no account of transcription, coding, analyst roles, reflexivity, theme derivation, saturation, or prevalence. A few quotations cannot substantiate the broad design recommendations. Convenience sampling largely from NLP/computational-social-science researchers also limits generalization to practicing qualitative researchers.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence. Table 2 does not support the stated “greater distinctiveness” of synchronous Climate codebooks; Table 10 labels values as percentages above 0.3 while the prose interprets them as below 0.3; and the Climate relational and LLM tables contain identical codebooks without explaining whether codebooks were reused, which bears directly on experimental independence.

Although the collected artifacts could support an informative exploratory case study, the paper's causal and general claims are not presently sound enough for Findings. Addressing the stated aims requires a matched asynchronous-collaboration condition, substantially more independent groups, controlled effort and assignment, hierarchical inference, and validated evaluation measures—substantial work likely extending beyond the next review cycle.
